interactions.summary: The class tests whether all good novelists summon real characters; Jiang says real fiction feels true because it communicates universal truths, while bad writers simply make things up and good writers are chosen rather than self-appointed.

A student links lightness to spiritual ideas and heaviness to material worry, and Jiang affirms this by saying hell's depth corresponds to mechanization and loss of connection to universal consciousness.
A student objects that the theory seems to destroy imagination by making every fictional person pre-existing and leaving nothing genuinely new under the sun.

claims.claim: Jiang says fiction feels real because it explains universal truths rather than because it invents arbitrary novelty.
Jiang distinguishes good from bad writers by ontological access: bad writers make things up, while good writers are chosen and have a stronger connection to the divine.
He makes the strong deterministic-sounding claim that true writers are born that way and chosen by God rather than becoming writers through ambition or will alone.
Jiang accepts the student's intuition that spiritual lightness improves access to ideas, while material heaviness narrows thought toward scarcity and obligation.
He glosses Lucifer at the bottom of hell as a machine that has lost consciousness because it has lost connection to universal consciousness.

signature_moments.moment: The writer is not self-made but chosen, and wanting fame is almost proof of bad writing.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows how radically Jiang sacralizes artistic vocation.

signature_moments.moment: Hell bottoms out in a machine because severance from universal consciousness is the deepest damnation.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives Jiang a memorable metaphysical image for spiritual deadness.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's account of authentic artistic vocation as divine election rather than career choice.
What real fiction discloses, making it feel true to readers rather than merely fabricated.
Jiang's metaphor for a being cut off from higher consciousness and reduced to automatic material functioning.

chronology_notes.note: The June 26 lecture now extends the summoning theory from Dante and Virgil into a broader theology of vocation, artistic truth, and mechanized damnation.
